newsitem.title: USA: US must bear some of burden for DC programs - Board.
newsitem.headline: US must bear some of burden for DC programs - Board.

text.p: The District of Columbia Control Board will tell the U.S. Congress on Thursday that it must take over some of the financial burden of key D.C. programs, including possibly prisons, Medicaid, mental health care, and roads and bridges maintenance.

"The authority is convinced that one of the most basic reasons for the District's continued financial problems is that the nation's capital is not supported -- as is every other city in the United States -- by a state," the five-member board said in a draft strategic plan for the ailing city that it is scheduled to release tomorrow.
A draft of the report was obtained by Reuters on Wednesday.

The panel said, "states ... relieve some of the burdens on their cities in numerous ways for which the District has no recourse. The burden and costs that other states bear for their cities need to be borne for this city by the federal government."

The Control Board said it will recommend by March 31 options for a more equitable structure, including the possibilities of the federal government assuming more of the costs of prisons, Medicaid, mental health care and infrastructure mainenance.
The five-member board said that by January 31 next year it will make recommendations to Congress and the White House to help the city deal with its unfunded pension liability.
The board said that in 1979, the federal government transferred the pension plans for police officers, firefighters and teachers, and a $2 billion unfunded liability to the District.

Under the plan, the District must take full responsibility for the unfunded pension programs by 2004, when the unfunded liability is expected to baloon from the current $4.7 billion to over $7 billion.
"Without some change in the law, the impact ... on the District's operating budget will be catastrophic," the Control Board said in the 25-page draft report.
The Control Board said it will make additional recommendations for "long-term improvements" in the current structure of city finances by September 30.
Also by September 30 the board will make specific recommendations for reorganizing the city's government and restructuring its delivery of services.
